studies.title: Labouring And Still Weary
studies.meaning: The surah opens as a question put to one listener, and the day is named by a participle meaning something that covers over, without saying what it covers. Then the description begins with faces, not with people, because a face is where a state is read. The third line holds the difficulty: working and worn out. Classical commentators differ over when that labour happened, some placing it in this life as effort spent on nothing, others inside the punishment itself, and the sources keep both readings.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah belongs to the period when the case for a reckoning was being made to people who granted that God created and denied that He would judge. Its method is not argument but presentation: two panels, two sets of faces, no transition between them. The classical sources record no occasion of revelation for the opening lines and treat the whole chapter as a single unbroken piece.

keyTerms.note: An active participle of covering something completely. The Quran uses this word twice; the other place applies it to a punishment that arrives and covers people, so the name carries suddenness as well as scale.

From the root behind stillness in prayer. The same word describes the composure of someone standing before God, so the humbling here is the involuntary version of a posture that was once available by choice.
An active participle of toil that wears a body down. Paired with the word for working, it gives labour and its cost in two beats, with no result named between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wasted labour was a real and specific fear. A well dug through rock for a season might come up dry. A caravan financed on borrowed money could reach Syria to find the price collapsed. Men returned from such ventures thinner, and the household read the outcome off their faces before anyone spoke. The surah uses that exact sequence: first the face, then the work, then what the work was worth.
studies.didYouKnow: The classical collections preserve a well-known report that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) used to recite this surah together with the one immediately before it at the Friday gathering and at the two festival prayers. The pairing meant that whole towns heard these two chapters side by side several times a year, which is why they are so often learned together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Effort is separated from worth. The passage does not describe idle people being punished; it describes people who worked hard, and it lets that stand without softening. What was missing was direction, not exertion. The consequence reaches further than the scene: a life can be strenuous, disciplined and admired, and still be spent on nothing, and no amount of internal effort settles the question by itself.

crossReferences.why: Names the greatest losers as those whose effort went astray while they thought they were doing well.
Turns completed deeds into scattered dust, the same gap between labour expended and value retained.
Uses another name for the same day, the overwhelming calamity, and also opens with its arrival.

studies.applyIt: Name the thing that tired you most this week. Say it out loud if you can. Then ask one question about it, not whether it was worth the money but whether you would want it counted. You are not obliged to change anything today. Just make sure you know which of your efforts you would want to keep.

studies.title: Pleased With Their Striving
studies.meaning: The food is defined entirely by failure. It does not fatten and it does not answer hunger, two negatives with no positive content between them, so what is described is a provision that is not one. Classical commentators identify the plant as a thorn that grazing animals refuse once it dries. Then, with no transition, the same opening word returns and everything reverses. The first quality given to the other group is not a pleasure. It is satisfaction with their own striving.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah runs two panels in sequence, and this passage is the seam between them. Its audience knew famine as a recurring event rather than a disaster, and knew exactly which plants people fell back on in a bad year. The classical sources give no occasion for these lines and read them as the pivot on which the whole chapter turns.

keyTerms.note: A desert plant named only here in the Quran. Lexicographers describe it as harmless while green and refused by camels once dry, so the word already carried the sense of something eaten only in desperation.
From the root of softness and comfort, used of skin that has been well kept. It answers the earlier word for humbled faces at the level of texture, so the contrast is physical before it is moral.
The noun is effort exerted, the same root as hurrying between the two hills. The line makes the object of their satisfaction their own work, not the reward, which is the harder thing to say.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a failed year people ate what the herds left. There were named plants that filled a stomach without feeding anyone, and everyone knew which ones they were and what it meant when a family started on them. Camels browsing thorn scrub were an ordinary sight; a person doing the same was a marker of how bad things had become. The image needed no explanation to a first audience.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah gives the two groups unequal space. Six ayat describe the first set of faces and nine describe the second, and the longer of the two panels is the one about the garden. The imbalance is visible on the page: a chapter that opens on an overwhelming day spends more of itself on rest than on fire.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is described as approval rather than compensation. Being pleased with your striving means the effort itself is returned to you as something good, which is a different claim from being paid for it. The passage sets that against a punishment defined as intake without nourishment. Both sides are described in terms of whether what a person took in did anything, and the moral weight sits in the outcome of effort, not in its quantity.

crossReferences.why: Says the same thing from God's side, that this is your reward and your striving has been appreciated.
Promises that righteous effort is not denied, using the same vocabulary of striving being written down.
Describes the other side's food in parallel terms, as something eaten only by those who refused.

studies.applyIt: At the end of today, name one thing you did that you would still be glad about in a year. Not the largest thing, the one that would last. Say it to yourself before you sleep, and let it be enough for the day. The passage makes that particular kind of satisfaction the first pleasure of the garden.

studies.title: No Idle Word Heard
studies.meaning: The first thing said about the garden is an absence, and it is an absence of speech. Classical commentators take the word for what is not heard to cover both empty chatter and talk that wounds, since the root runs from the useless to the false. Only after that do the furnishings arrive, four of them in a row, and every one is a passive participle: raised, set down, ranged, spread. Nothing is described being fetched or prepared. The place is found already arranged.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. This is the middle of the surah's second panel, and its vocabulary is drawn from the reception room of a wealthy household rather than from anything unimaginable. Mecca sat on a trade route, and imported textiles and vessels passed through it constantly. The classical sources record no occasion for these lines and note that the imagery works by taking the top of a familiar scale.

keyTerms.note: A participle from the root of cancelling something out. It covers speech that is merely empty and speech that does damage, so the absence removes both the pointless conversation and the cutting remark.
A passive participle of lifting. Couches set high were where a host seated the honoured guest, so the word carries rank and not merely height, and the rank is given rather than claimed.
A plural naming the small pillows placed for leaning against, and it appears nowhere else in the Quran. The detail is domestic: not thrones, but the bolsters of a room set out for a long evening.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A Meccan merchant's reception room was a display of the trade routes. Cups came up from the south or across from Persia, carpets from the Yemen, cushions covered in cloth that had travelled further than most people ever would. Guests were seated by rank, and the arrangement of a room said what the host thought of each man in it. Everything in this passage is that room, described as already waiting.
studies.didYouKnow: Four consecutive lines here end on the same grammatical form, a passive participle of the same pattern, so the rhyme and the grammar arrive together. The effect is that the furnishings are heard as a list of things done rather than things owned, and the agent is never named in any of the four.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Paradise is introduced by subtraction. Before any pleasure is named, a category of noise is removed, which makes peace a social condition rather than a private one. The passive participles carry the second point. Nobody in the garden arranged the garden, so the place is not an achievement being enjoyed but a hospitality being received, and the difference between those two is the whole tone of the passage.

crossReferences.why: Removes the same two kinds of speech and names what is heard instead, only peace repeated.
Makes the absence of idle talk the defining quality of the promised gardens of Eden.
Passes a cup between them that produces neither empty speech nor wrongdoing.

studies.applyIt: Pick one conversation today and leave out the part that was only going to be noise: the small correction, the story that puts you slightly ahead, the comment about someone absent. Say the rest normally. Afterwards notice how much shorter it was, and whether anything was actually lost by the cut.

studies.title: Look At The Camel
studies.meaning: The garden list closes with carpets, and then the surah turns outward into four questions built on the same word: how. How the camels were created, the sky raised, the mountains set, the earth spread. Every verb is passive, so each thing is presented as having been done to rather than as simply being there. Classical commentators note that the camel comes first because it stood in front of the audience daily. The argument is built from the ordinary, not from a marvel.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people who already granted that God made the world and refused the conclusion that He would raise them. Because the premise was shared, the surah does not argue for a creator; it asks for attention to what the premise implies. The classical sources report no occasion for these lines and read them as the turn from description of the last day back to the present one.

keyTerms.note: A collective noun with no singular of its own pattern. Arabic names the herd, and a single animal has to be called something else, so the line points at camels as a kind rather than at one beast.
A passive of planting something upright and firm, used of a tent pole driven in. It makes the mountains installed rather than piled, which is why the Quran elsewhere calls them pegs.
From the root of a surface or a flat roof. Commentators read it as the earth made level for living on, describing how the ground presents itself to someone standing and walking on it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A camel was a household's capital. It carried the load, gave milk through a drought, supplied hair for the tent and hide for the water skin, walked for days without drinking, and knelt to be loaded, which no other large animal in the region would do. Every person hearing these lines had watched one being loaded that morning. The passage points at the most familiar object in the street.
studies.didYouKnow: All four questions close on a passive verb, and all four of those verbs end on the same rhyme, so the grammatical form and the sound repeat together four times. The result is that the four objects arrive as a single sweep from the nearest thing to the widest, and no agent is named in any of them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation here asks for observation rather than assent. The four questions are not about whether the world was made but about how it is put together, which is a request to look rather than to agree. The passive voice does the theological work: a made thing implies a maker without the passage having to say so, and the reader is left to complete the sentence himself.

crossReferences.why: Gathers the same kind of everyday evidence, from ships to rain to winds, for people who reason.
Turns the same instruction inward, placing signs on the earth and then in the observer himself.
Details what the livestock actually provide, warmth, food, transport and beauty, in the same argument.

studies.applyIt: Choose one ordinary thing you pass every day without looking, a tree on your street, a bird on the wire, your own hand. Give it sixty seconds of attention to how it is put together, not what it means. The passage does not ask for a rare sight. It asks for a proper look at a common one.

studies.title: You Are Not Their Overseer
studies.meaning: Two limits are set in two lines. The role is to remind, stated with a restrictive particle that leaves nothing else in it, and then the authority to compel is denied outright with a rare and forceful word. What follows has long been discussed, since an exception clause about whoever turns away attaches awkwardly to a denial of control; readings run from taking it as a resumption of the command to treating the next line as a fresh sentence. Either way the reckoning is moved off the messenger.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the later years there, when rejection had settled into something permanent and the surahs repeatedly address the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in his own distress at it. Classical commentators read the passage as consolation rather than instruction: the community was small and had no power to impose anything on anyone, and the lines describe that condition as the intended one.

keyTerms.note: An active participle naming the person by the act, not by rank. It assumes the hearer already possesses what is being recalled, which makes the messenger's work retrieval rather than imposition.
A rare intensive form for someone set over others with power to compel. The root occurs only twice in the Quran, and in both places it is denied, once of a messenger and once of his opponents.
A verbal noun of coming back to where one started, rather than the ordinary word for returning. It frames the last day as arrival at an origin, which is why the line reads as settled fact.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nobody in Mecca held coercive power over anyone's belief. Authority ran through clan protection and reputation, and a chief led by consent that could be withdrawn. At the seasonal fairs a herald announced his message, took the mockery, and moved on; there was no apparatus behind him. The passage describes a situation the first audience could see with their own eyes, and names it as the arrangement rather than a shortfall.
studies.didYouKnow: The word denied to the Prophet here appears in only one other place in the Quran, where it is put as a question to his opponents: do they hold the treasuries of your Lord, or are they the controllers. The same rare word is refused to both sides of the argument, which leaves the role unoccupied by anyone.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Delivering a message and enforcing it are separated at the level of the messenger's job description, not as a concession to circumstance. That separation has consequences the passage does not spell out: if no compulsion belongs to the one who received the revelation directly, it belongs to nobody after him either. The reckoning is then reserved, and reserved in the first person, which removes it from every human hand.

crossReferences.why: Uses a different word for the same denial, that he is not a tyrant over them, and repeats the command to remind.
States the principle directly, that there is no compulsion in religion, and grounds it in clarity.
Asks whether he would compel people into belief, given that faith itself is not forced.

studies.applyIt: Think of the person you have been trying to convince of something, and count how many times you have made the case. Make it once more, carefully, and then stop for a month. Watch what the silence does. You are not withdrawing the argument. You are returning the decision to the person whose decision it is.

studies.title: The Reckoning Is Ours
studies.meaning: Four words close the surah, and the construction is the striking part. Arabic puts what someone owes on them with a preposition of burden, the form used for a debt or an undertaking, and here that form is used of God. Classical commentators read it not as an obligation imposed from outside but as a commitment freely taken on. The opening connector matters too, since it separates the reckoning from the return named in the line before. Arrival and accounting are two events. Nothing is said about the outcome.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has run from a day that covers everything, through two sets of faces, out to four things in the visible world, and then back to a messenger who cannot compel anyone. This last line ends that movement by handing the whole matter upward. The classical sources give no occasion for it and treat the closing pair of ayat as the chapter's resolution.

keyTerms.note: A connector implying sequence with an interval, unlike the simpler joining particle. It sets the accounting after the return rather than alongside it, so the two lines describe two moments and not one.
The preposition of what is owed, used in contracts for a debt resting on a party. Applied to God it is read as a self-undertaking, since nothing external can place a duty on Him.
From the root of counting and arithmetic, a commercial word before it was a religious one. It names an accounting that itemises, not a verdict simply announced at the end.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan trade ran on deferred settlement. Goods went north on credit, shares in a caravan were recorded, and accounts were squared when the season closed and the animals came back. Everyone understood that a return and a reckoning were separate occasions, sometimes weeks apart, and that the second was where a partnership was actually tested. The surah's last two lines use that exact sequence.
studies.didYouKnow: The final two ayat of this surah both switch God into the first person plural, after twenty-four lines that have spoken of Him in the third person, including the punishment named just before. The chapter ends closer to the speaker than it began, and the shift lands on the two words about return and reckoning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Judgement is presented as something God undertakes rather than delegates, which closes the surah's argument about the messenger from the other end. If no one is a controller over anyone, the accounting cannot be devolved either. The line also withholds the verdict. It promises that the books will be opened and says nothing at all about what is in them, which leaves fear and hope both standing.

crossReferences.why: Divides the same two tasks explicitly, delivery belonging to the messenger and the reckoning to God.
Describes the accounting itself, scales set in place and nothing omitted, however small the weight.
Uses the same construction of self-undertaking, where mercy is written upon Himself.

studies.applyIt: Settle one small open account today. The apology you never finished, the money you meant to return, the message left unanswered for a month. Pick the one you have been carrying longest and close it before tonight. Accounts that stay open get heavier, and this one is still small enough to clear in a few minutes.
